transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-09-21 15:30 PDT / Duration ~54 minutes / Attendees: Avery (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Rachel (Skyline Head of ML), Samir (Platform Eng), Noah (CTO)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery to validate how close outputs and perf look when porting from Anthropic/OpenAI + vLLM/TGI to Redwood Hosted/Dedicated/Private. Discussed security, PKI/KMS, tokenization differences and batch/kv cache impacts. Agreed to a small parity pilot and to share artifacts.

[00:00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Avery from Redwood, AE on this account, and with me is Diego, one of our solutions engineers. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:08] Rachel: Good, thanks. Running a bit behind but ready to dig in.
[00:00:11] Noah: Hey, thanks. We tried to allocate more time, appreciate it.
[00:00:15] Diego: Awesome, quick agenda—we want to understand your existing stack, major constraints, and then talk about how we approach parity runs and pilots. We'll surface common gotchas like tokenization, kv cache differences, and private deploy needs.
[00:00:28] Samir: Sounds good. For context, Skyline runs a hybrid stack—most prod workloads call Anthropic for safety-sensitive chat and OpenAI for bulk summarization. For latency-sensitive features we front with an internal stack using vLLM and TGI layered on GKE.
[00:00:44] Rachel: The goal is to evaluate whether we can consolidate to a single inference provider that gives us predictable latency and lower unit cost without regression on eval sets. We're also picky about logging, retention and KMS control.
[00:00:56] Avery: Perfect, that's exactly what Redwood's built for — hosted for quick wins, dedicated for predictable throughput, and private for VPC/on-prem. Quick question: how mature is your vLLM/TGI setup? Are you doing custom kernels or standard builds?
[00:01:12] Samir: Uh, mostly standard vLLM builds with a couple of custom tweaks for KV eviction and our batching hook. We've hacked in a custom tokenizer mapping to match Anthropic token counts — that's been a pain.
[00:01:25] Diego: Right, tokenizer differences are a huge source of eval delta. We often map tokenizers and re-tokenize eval prompts to compare apples-to-apples. If you have custom mapping, we'd want to review that.
[00:01:37] Rachel: Yeah, we've got a tokenizer shim. But even then, sometimes the output text differs because of subtokenization. We need generation parity on our 3 core prompt suites: summarize-reply, doc-extract, and persona-chat.
[00:01:50] Noah: Also, we measure unit economics at per-request and per-token levels. If we move to Redwood Dedicated, we need clear numbers: cost per 1k tokens at our observed RTTs and throughput.
[00:02:01] Avery: Totally. Diego, want to walk through how we approach parity runs?
[00:02:05] Diego: Sure. Typically we set up a pilot environment that mirrors your traffic—small sample first. We ingest your eval sets, run them across the target model versions in Redwood (hosted and dedicated) and compare metrics: token counts, alignment scores, latency P50/P95, and cost. We also instrument KV cache behavior and matching batch sizes. Two common surprises: batch shaping—if your vLLM custom batch hook is doing dynamic micro-batches, we need to mimic that; and prefix caching—some hosts keep a warm KV cache which changes latency on first token vs sustained throughput.
[00:02:41] Rachel: Can Redwood replicate our vLLM caching behavior? We rely on keeping long conversation KV for chat, and we suspect that’s one reason our Anthropic outputs feel more consistent.
[00:02:52] Diego: We have a KV/prefix caching layer and can configure TTLs and pinning for sessions. On Dedicated and Private we give more control—on Hosted we use a policy that balances memory and cost. For the pilot we'd match your TTLs.
[00:03:05] Samir: And quantization — we run int8 for some models in vLLM. Does Redwood support the same quantized kernels on Dedicated?
[00:03:12] Avery: Yes, we support quantized variants and have guidance on which quant profiles preserve quality. Diego, maybe you can add specifics?
[00:03:17] Diego: On our runtime we support int8 and a couple of proprietary quant profiles. The kernel selection depends on architecture and sequence lengths. We also have a guardrail: when we detect quality regressions beyond your threshold, we can fallback to FP16 on the fly.
[00:03:32] Noah: Interesting. About private deployment — we have to keep keys on our KMS and restrict network egress. Is Redwood Private able to integrate with customer-managed KMS and no-egress policy?
[00:03:44] Avery: Yes, for Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and the control plane is optional to host — we can do a customer-managed control plane. You can also choose air-gapped on-prem installs.
[00:03:56] Rachel: Audit logs and retention—SOC2 requirement. We need immutable logs, and we need log retention for up to seven years for some clients. Can you surface token-level traceability?
[00:04:07] Diego: We capture request traces, model version, token counts and decision traces. For Hosted we retain logs per plan; for Dedicated and Private you control retention. We can stream audit logs to your S3 or SIEM for long-term retention.
[00:04:20] Samir: Ok, the next sticky area is function calling and tools—we use structured tool calls with Anthropic function-style JSONs. Does Redwood preserve structured outputs and guarantee schema stability?
[00:04:32] Avery: Yes, our API supports structured output and tool calling. We can pin model versions and provide deterministic settings to reduce hallucination. We also support output validators at the SDK level which can enforce schema at inference time.
[00:04:45] Rachel: Great. For the pilot, we want to run our three eval suites across two model families—one from the Anthropic-canonical set and one from the OpenAI-style family—and then a smaller in-house fine-tuned variant.
[00:04:58] Diego: That's doable. One practical note: when you bring a fine-tuned model that was trained against Anthropic tokenization quirks, you might see delta. We recommend re-finetune or apply a tokenizer shim as part of the data preproc for the pilot.
[00:05:12] Noah: How do you handle incumbent vendor fallbacks? If we have a hybrid route during migration where some requests still go to Anthropic/OpenAI, can Redwood route by policy?
[00:05:22] Avery: Yes, smart routing is built-in. You can route by latency targets, cost, region, or customer tier. We can set a fallback policy that sends a request to your legacy vendor only on specific failure modes.
[00:05:33] Samir: On networking, we need mutual TLS to your endpoints for Dedicated. Do you support client certs?
[00:05:39] Diego: We do for Dedicated and Private. Hosted supports mTLS via dedicated peering/privatelink-style connections in the cloud regions.
[00:05:48] Rachel: Can we talk about typical SLOs? Our internal bar is P95 < 220ms for short-turn use-cases (<=128 tokens) and P95 < 500ms for medium-turn. Can Redwood meet that?
[00:06:01] Avery: Depends on the model and the hardware profile. On Dedicated we guarantee latency targets with reserved GPU pools and autoscaling policies. We can provision a configuration to hit your P95s—Diego, we have a note on the NVLink families and sequence-length tuned kernels?
[00:06:13] Diego: Yep. For short sequences, certain AMP kernels and attention optimizations matter. We'll match your model architecture to the hardware profile and run a small latency sweep. In our experience, with matching batch sizes and warm KV caches, P95 for 128 tokens on A100-class hardware is sub-200ms for many chat models. But again, quantization and tokenizer differences can change generation time.
[00:06:34] Noah: For the pilot, we want to measure not just latency but also deterministic output parity. How do you score that?
[00:06:40] Diego: We use a mix: exact match for extraction tasks, BLEU/ROUGE-type metrics for summarization plus semantic similarity scores (embedding-based), and a human evaluation bucket for persona/chat where small changes matter. We'll surface per-prompt diffs and annotate where output drift is acceptable vs blocking.
[00:07:00] Rachel: Human eval budget—do you run that or do we provide labels?
[00:07:04] Avery: We can help run small human evals as an add-on or you can provide labels. For the initial parity, customers usually do a lightweight 50–200 human checks on borderline prompts.
[00:07:14] Samir: A practical point: our dev stack uses a homegrown SDK with request batching and a pre-tokenization step. During the pilot, do we need to change SDKs or can you accept raw token streams?
[00:07:25] Diego: We support both. For parity, it's easiest to re-play your request traces through Redwood's SDK so we can replicate batching and tokenization exactly. If you prefer to send raw token streams, we can accept them but then we need exact token boundaries.
[00:07:38] Rachel: Would prefer minimal engineering changes if possible.
[00:07:40] Avery: We'll try to keep client changes minimal—our pilot checklist includes a traffic replay mode. Diego will own the replay runbook.
[00:07:47] [00:07:50] — short side conversation —
[00:07:50] Noah: (low) Are we comfortable rolling this into infra roadmap Q4 if numbers look good?
[00:07:54] Rachel: (low) Depends on pilot results and security checks.
[00:07:58] Avery: Quick note on pricing—pilot can run on Hosted credits or Dedicated trial nodes depending on throughput. We'll propose both in the SOW.
[00:08:10] Samir: What's your typical pilot length?
[00:08:12] Diego: Two weeks is common for parity; if we need more data, we extend to four. For Skyline I'd recommend two-week parity plus one-week follow-up.
[00:08:21] Rachel: Ok good. A couple of vendor concerns—are there any known gaps moving from TGI/vLLM to Redwood? For example, custom prefetch or eviction semantics that we implemented in vLLM.
[00:08:33] Diego: The gap tends to be in low-level runtime hooks. vLLM allows deep customizations, and if you're relying on those, we can either replicate via our runtime extension points on Dedicated/Private or run a compatibility shim during the pilot.
[00:08:49] Samir: About telemetry—we need token-level cost attribution back to product teams. Does Redwood provide per-route/token cost breakdowns by default?
[00:08:58] Avery: Redwood Console surfaces token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route and model. You can export granular reports and set alerts on cost drift.
[00:09:08] Rachel: Great. Any limitations on model formats? We have a couple of models exported as ggml and some as safetensors.
[00:09:16] Diego: We take safetensors and standard transformer checkpoints. For ggml, we usually need to convert to supported formats; we have tooling and can assist. For fine-tuned artifacts, we'll request a small sample to validate.
[00:09:28] Noah: What's your approach to rollback/failsafe—if we see quality regressions after rolling out?
[00:09:33] Avery: Rollouts support canaries, A/B, and automatic fallback to a compatible variant. We'll set up automatic health checks and a rollback policy in the console.
[00:09:44] Rachel: Okay let's sketch the immediate pilot scope and criteria on the call: 1) Run 3 eval suites across 3 model variants, 2) measure P50/P95 latencies and cost per 1k tokens, 3) human eval 100 prompts for persona-chat, threshold 90% pass, 4) integration test for function calling schema.
[00:10:06] Diego: I'll note that. We'll produce a parity report with diffs, metrics and suggested remediations.
[00:10:12] Samir: A few infra asks — we need a sandbox VPC that has strict egress rules and a KMS key we manage. Also, can we get a stubbed audit log sink for testing?
[00:10:23] Avery: Yes to all. For the sandbox VPC we usually provide a CloudFormation/Terraform template. Diego will send the template and the minimal IAM roles.
[00:10:33] Rachel: For timelines, we have a stakeholder review on 2026-10-18 and would like pilot results before that. Can we aim to start first week of October and wrap by 10/11?
[00:10:44] Avery: That's feasible. We'll aim to kick off 2026-10-04 and have results by 2026-10-11.
[00:10:49] Noah: Any blockers to starting?
[00:10:51] Samir: I need to confirm access constraints with security; otherwise main blocker is the tokenizer shim and sample eval sets.
[00:10:59] Rachel: I'll gather the eval sets and send them.
[00:11:02] Avery: Great. Any other technical deep dives you want to reserve for a subsequent session? We can do a kernel/quantization deep-dive with our runtime folks.
[00:11:11] Rachel: Yes, let's schedule the quantization/kernel deep-dive. That'll include your runtime lead and our ML infra lead.
[00:11:18] Avery: Noted. Diego, anything else to add?
[00:11:21] Diego: One last note—small differences can be amplified if prompt templating differs. We'll ask for the exact prompt wrappers you use and also a sample of pre/post-processing to keep the pipeline consistent. Also, if you use instruction-weighting or safety filters upstream, capture those as part of the eval.
[00:11:36] Samir: Understood. We'll provide prompt wrappers and the policy filters.
[00:11:40] Avery: Ok let's recap and close out: 1) Avery to send pricing and SOW and parity template by 9/24; 2) Diego to send Terraform sandbox VPC template and tokenizer/quant notes by 9/27; 3) Rachel to provide eval sets and prompt wrappers by 9/23; 4) Samir to provision sandbox access by 9/29. We'll schedule pilot kickoff for 2026-10-04.
[00:12:05] Rachel: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[00:12:07] Noah: Thanks.
[00:12:09] Diego: Thanks, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the SOW.
[00:12:12] Avery: Appreciate it—bye all.

Notes on transcript quality: some acronyms mis-transcribed (TGI -> "T G I" in places), tokenizer spelled out sometimes, occasional speaker label noise.

Referenced artifacts/links: parity-benchmark-template.xlsx (link pending from Avery), sandbox-vpc-terraform.zip (to be shared by Diego), Redwood security brief (SOC2 + KMS integration) link (to be shared).

End of meeting.
